planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Marumi is among the most cold-hardy kumquats and, like other kumquats, is eaten whole, skin and all, since the sweet rind contrasts with tart flesh.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Marumi is one of the oldest kumquat cultivars grown, producing small, round fruit with thin, sweet, edible skin surrounding a tarter, seedier pulp, eaten whole rather than peeled. It is among the more cold-hardy kumquats and, being a naturally small, dense shrub, adapts well to container culture and can be moved under cover during hard freezes in the cooler parts of its range. Fruit ripens in winter and holds on the tree for weeks without dropping, giving a long, flexible harvest window; established plants are otherwise low-maintenance and require only routine citrus fertilizing.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Rainbow is a variegated selection of native drooping leucothoe with cream, pink, and copper mottled new growth that is showier in some shade than in deep, dark shade.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can scorch the variegated foliage. Rainbow is a colorful sport of the native Appalachian shrub drooping leucothoe, with glossy, arching evergreen leaves splashed in cream, pink, and coppery-red that are showiest on new growth in spring and again in cool fall weather. Small, white, urn-shaped flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in spring, similar to its relatives in the heath family. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a graceful, cascading mound, making it a good textural companion for ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials, and benefits from an occasional thinning of old canes at the base to keep growth vigorous.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; the tightly ruffled, crimped leaf margins of Crispatum make it one of the most distinctive-textured leopard plant cultivars for a shady bed or large container.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh sun that can scorch the leaves. Crispatum is a striking cultivar of Farfugium japonicum, the Gulf Coast garden staple known as leopard plant, selected for round leaves with tightly crimped, ruffled margins that give the foliage an almost sculptural, parsley-like texture unlike the flatter leaves of the species. Clusters of small, daisy-like yellow flowers rise above the foliage on tall stems in fall. It spreads slowly into a dense clump, tolerates deep shade better than most broadleaf perennials, and is a favorite container and border plant in Southern shade gardens for its bold, unusual texture.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; unlike its relative wild ginger, Saruma has upright stems rather than a low creeping habit and self-seeds modestly in a favorable woodland setting.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade. Saruma henryi is a monotypic Chinese woodland genus closely related to wild ginger, but unlike its low, creeping cousin it grows upright stems clothed in heart-shaped, softly hairy leaves, forming a small clump rather than a mat. In late spring it produces small, nodding, pale yellow flowers shaped much like those of wild ginger, followed by modest self-seeding in a hospitable shade garden. It combines well with hostas, ferns, and hellebores in a woodland border, tolerates a range of shade conditions once established, and needs little care beyond a yearly topdressing of leaf compost.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Tea Oil Camellia is notably more cold-hardy than most ornamental camellias and its late-fall bloom often escapes damage from early frosts.

directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Grown for centuries in China for the edible oil pressed from its seeds, Tea Oil Camellia produces fragrant white flowers in late fall into winter and is notably more cold-hardy than the familiar ornamental camellias, tolerating temperatures well below what damages Camellia japonica or sasanqua. The glossy evergreen foliage and modest size make it a useful dual-purpose shrub for a partly shaded border, valued both as an ornamental flowering evergreen and, where enough plants are grown, for pressing the oil-rich seeds. It tolerates a range of light conditions from woodland shade to fairly sunny sites and needs the same acidic soil and good drainage as other camellias.
